vignette:
She is an 80-year-old African woman who has spent most of her life speaking hope into other people’s suffering. In her church, people know her as “Mama Pastor,” a steady presence with a warm handshake, a practiced smile, and prayers that seem to arrive exactly when they are needed. It takes several meetings before she begins to speak in detail about the years when she herself had no steady ground under her feet.

She grows up in a small town where family life is crowded, noisy, and ordinary in the ways she now misses most: women pounding grain in the morning, children running between houses, the smell of cooking fires at dusk. She marries young, and by the time violence begins spreading through the region, she and her husband already have children to protect. At first, she tells herself the unrest is temporary. People whisper names, disappearances, threats. Then one night the fear becomes undeniable. Armed men come through nearby homes, and the sounds she remembers most clearly are not the shouting but the smaller sounds underneath it: a child screaming for his mother, feet slamming against packed earth, the crackle of something burning.

She and her family flee quickly, carrying very little. She remembers forcing herself not to look back for long because if she really sees the house, the trees, the doorway, she is afraid she will freeze. During the journey, she learns to live inside a kind of alertness that never fully leaves her. She scans faces. She counts children again and again. She sleeps lightly, if at all. Even now, decades later, she speaks of that time with her shoulders tight and her hands folded so firmly that her knuckles pale. She remembers hunger, waiting, and the humiliation of depending on strangers for scraps of information and permission to move. In the refugee camp, she tries to be useful—helping other women, praying with the sick, organizing children into small circles of song and scripture when there is nothing else to give them. She says faith keeps her alive, but she also admits there are nights when she feels abandoned by God and then hates herself for thinking it.

Eventually, the family is resettled. Safety comes, but not the kind that settles into her body. She learns a new country in pieces: bus routes, grocery stores, official forms, winter coats. Her husband finds work first. She becomes known in the church community because she listens well, remembers everyone’s losses, and can speak about survival without sounding proud of it. Over time, she is ordained and begins serving formally as a pastor. To others, her life looks redeemed by purpose. She is grateful, and she is also tired in a way she cannot explain.

In the present, she still startles sharply at loud knocks, sirens, or the sound of people arguing outside. If she hears raised voices in a parking lot, her heart begins to race before her mind catches up. At night she often wakes from dreams in which she is running and cannot gather the children fast enough. Sometimes in the dream she is back at the house, trying to choose what to carry while smoke thickens the doorway; sometimes she is in a crowd and one of her children is suddenly missing. She wakes disoriented, drenched in sweat, and needs several moments to remind herself of her age, her room, her husband sleeping beside her.

She avoids news footage of war because it pulls her in too quickly. Even short clips of people carrying bundles or standing behind fences can stay with her for days. On Sundays, if a congregant begins describing political violence back home, she remains outwardly composed, but later she finds herself unable to rest. She paces the kitchen, checks the locks twice, and listens for sounds that do not belong in her quiet neighborhood. Her husband tells her she is safe now. She believes him in her mind, but her body does not.

She carries guilt that has aged with her. She wonders about the neighbors who did not escape, about relatives she could not help, about whether she did enough for her children when fear made her impatient and hard. She speaks gently to grieving families in her congregation, yet she is harsher with herself than she would ever be with them. She says there is a part of her that never unpacked, a part still standing ready to run.

What pains her most is how hidden this remains. People see strength, wisdom, endurance. They do not see how crowded her inner life is with images she never invited back. When church members praise her resilience, she nods and thanks them. Then she goes home, sits in silence, and waits for her breathing to slow.
